content: The dapivirine vaginal ring demonstrated approximately 30% efficacy in reducing HIV infection in an intention-to-treat analysis. However, subgroup analysis by age revealed no significant efficacy among women aged 18–24 years, likely due to lower adherence rates. Results from two open-label extension studies, DREAM and HOPE, showed increased efficacy, adherence, and retention compared to the randomized controlled trials. One of these studies reported a 62% reduction in HIV transmission when compared to a simulated control. Further studies are ongoing to determine whether the lack of efficacy in younger women is due to non-adherence or other factors and to identify strategies to support adherence in this demographic. Safety and acceptability are also being studied in women aged 15–19 years, who were not included in the initial trials. The dapivirine vaginal ring acts locally, with minimal systemic absorption. Trials reported no significant differences in adverse events related to pregnancy, fetal outcomes, or infant outcomes between the treatment and placebo groups. However, due to the small number of pregnancies observed, ongoing trials are collecting additional safety data during pregnancy and breastfeeding. A meta-analysis of HIV infection outcomes from two Phase III placebo-controlled trials (ASPIRE and the Ring Study) found a 29% reduction in HIV risk (95% CI: 11–43%). A pooled analysis using time-to-event data from both trials reported a 27% relative reduction in HIV risk (95% CI: 9–42%). Individually, ASPIRE showed a 27% reduction (95% CI: 1–46%), and the Ring Study showed a 33% reduction (95% CI: 5–53%). In ASPIRE, efficacy increased to 37% (95% CI: 12–56%) when data from two low-adherence sites were excluded. Age-stratified analysis in ASPIRE revealed no significant risk reduction among women under 25 years (10% reduction, 95% CI: −41% to +43%), while women aged 25 years and older experienced a 61% reduction (95% CI: 32–77%). A post hoc analysis found no efficacy and lower adherence among women aged 18–21 years. The Ring Study also conducted an age-stratified analysis but found no significant differences in risk reduction between women aged 21 years and younger versus those older than 21 years. However, pooled results from both trials showed significantly higher risk reduction among participants older than 21 years, with no observed risk reduction for those aged 21 years or younger. The open-label extension studies DREAM and HOPE demonstrated increased efficacy, adherence, and retention compared to the randomized controlled trials. DREAM reported a 62% reduction in HIV risk compared to a simulated control, while HOPE showed a 39% relative reduction (95% CI: 14–69%). In HOPE, 92% of participants accepted the dapivirine vaginal ring at enrollment, and 73% continued its use throughout the study. Adverse event rates were similar across study arms, with moderate-certainty evidence at 24 months. Social harm related to study participation was reported in ASPIRE, with 94 instances of social harm over 4680 person-years of follow-up. Most cases (93%) were partner-related, often triggered by the partner discovering the ring during sexual activity or suspecting it was associated with ill health or infidelity. Consequences included ring destruction, physical violence, or relationship termination. Younger women (18–26 years) were more than twice as likely to experience social harm compared to older women, and social harm was associated with short-term decreases in product adherence. Resistance to NNRTIs was analyzed in ASPIRE, the Ring Study, DREAM, and HOPE. Among seroconverters, the prevalence of NNRTI-resistant infections ranged from 10% to 28%. Pregnancy incidence was similar between the dapivirine vaginal ring and placebo arms across all studies. However, significant differences in pregnancy incidence were observed based on contraceptive method, with higher rates among women using oral contraceptive pills compared to implants or injectables. Pregnancy-related outcomes showed no differences in adverse outcomes between the dapivirine vaginal ring and placebo arms. All studies required participants to use stable contraception, as the safety of dapivirine during pregnancy and breastfeeding remains unknown. Monthly pregnancy tests were conducted, and participants discontinued the study product if they became pregnant. Behavioral outcomes, including the number of sexual partners and condom use, were assessed in one study site in Uganda. No significant changes in non-condom use at last sex were observed between baseline and week 104. Similarly, the proportion of participants reporting two or more sexual partners remained stable over time. Four studies reported on the incidence of curable sexually transmitted infections, with no differences between study arms. However, one site in the Ring Study observed significant decreases in diagnoses of Trichomonas vaginalis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections over 104 weeks. The current production cost of the dapivirine vaginal ring is approximately $7 per ring. In lowand middle-income countries, it is anticipated that the ring will be provided free of charge at public health facilities. Modeling studies suggest that the ring may be more cost-effective than oral PrEP, as it requires fewer health system resources. A study in South Africa found that prioritizing the ring for female sex workers in KwaZulu-Natal would be cost-saving. Another modeling study indicated that the ring could have a modest impact on the HIV epidemic and be cost-effective, even with low efficacy, if uniform coverage across high-risk groups is achieved. The dapivirine vaginal ring is relatively easy to transport and store, as it does not require refrigeration and can be kept at room temperature. Several countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Kenya, South Africa, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, are considering initial steps for implementation. Acceptability studies found that the ring was highly acceptable, with most women reporting it was easy to insert and remove. Over time, acceptability increased as women became more comfortable using the ring and as it became more common in their communities. Concerns included hygiene during menstruation, potential health risks, the ring getting lost or stuck, and partner reactions. Most women disclosed ring use to their male partners, although some feared violence or anger if discovered. The ring was not felt by 70–92% of participants during sexual intercourse and by 48–97% of male partners. The introduction of the dapivirine vaginal ring as an additional HIV prevention option is expected to increase equity by providing a discrete, woman-controlled biomedical prevention method. Expanding PrEP options to include the ring could address the diverse needs and preferences of women. Evidence from contraception studies suggests that increasing prevention options may lead to increased use. Access to the ring could also provide additional opportunities for sexual and reproductive health services. The Guideline Development Group issued a conditional recommendation in favor of the dapivirine vaginal ring, assessing that the benefits likely outweigh the harms based on moderate-certainty evidence.
